questions.q: What is the main purpose of assigning a severity level (like SEV1-SEV4) to an incident?
options: To decide which team gets blamed for the outage
To remove the need to debate, under pressure, how big a deal something is before the right amount of urgency and staffing kicks in
To calculate the exact dollar cost of the incident before any response begins
Severity levels are purely cosmetic labels with no effect on response
questions.explain: Severity tiers let the right response — staffing, urgency, communication — happen immediately and consistently, without first arguing about how serious the problem is.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that the Incident Commander and Communications Lead should typically be different people during a serious incident?
options: Only the Communications Lead is legally allowed to talk to customers
Having one person both drive the technical fix and handle outward-facing updates pulls their attention in opposite directions at the exact moment focus matters most
The Incident Commander is not technical enough to answer stakeholder questions
Company policy at most firms requires exactly four named roles at all times
questions.explain: Splitting the roles keeps the technical responder from being interrupted for status updates, while the Communications Lead keeps stakeholders informed without needing to touch the investigation.

questions.q: In the illustrative timeline, what role does the Scribe play during the incident?
options: They write the final blog post announcing the outage to customers
They decide which severity level to assign before anyone else is notified
They perform the technical rollback once a cause is identified
They keep a real-time, timestamped log of what happened and when, which becomes the factual record used later
questions.explain: The Scribe's running log is what makes an accurate postmortem possible later — nobody can reconstruct exact timing from memory after the fact.

questions.q: In the lesson's timeline, why is the gap between detection (00:00) and a confirmed cause (00:12) called the most expensive part of the incident?
options: Because that is legally the only time window counted against the SLA
It isn't expensive — the most expensive period is always after the incident is already resolved
Because that's the window where the error budget is bleeding fastest, before any mitigation has started
Because that is when the postmortem document must be written
questions.explain: Until a cause is found and mitigation starts, the problem keeps consuming the error budget at full speed — which is why fast triage and clear roles matter more in the moment than deep root-cause analysis.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between an incident being "mitigated" and being "closed"?
options: Mitigated means the symptom has stopped; closed means the team has confirmed it's staying stopped before moving to postmortem work
There is no difference; the two terms are interchangeable
Closed happens first, then mitigated happens afterward as a formality
Mitigated applies only to SEV1 incidents, and closed applies only to SEV4 incidents
questions.explain: Mitigation stops the bleeding; closure confirms the fix held over time, at which point the incident hands off to the next lesson's postmortem process.
